headline: Northeastern University researchers have formed a group of more than 40 academics to build tools that could show when an AI chatbot is being deceptive.
score_reason: Kept at the pool score: a new international research group on AI deception, but it has no results yet and the article is the university's own account.
importance_line: People who use chatbots for medical, money or life advice could eventually get a way to tell when an answer is misleading, but the group has only started, no working detector or timetable is reported, and the account comes from the university itself.
summary: Northeastern Global News, the university's own news service, reports that computer scientist David Bau and colleagues have formed the International Consortium for Interpretable AI, more than 40 academics who share AI models, test methods and computing power to work out how AI systems reach their answers, which researchers say they do not fully understand. The aim is a 'white box' tool, in effect a lie detector that would spot patterns in a model's inner activity showing it is deceiving a user, and Bau's team has begun collecting data on when chatbots show sycophancy (telling users what they want to hear) in answering medical questions.
notes: Read in full. A university news feature built from its own researchers' statements: no outside experts, no results, no date for the consortium's formation. The headline is a question; the article does not claim a lie detector exists.
